title: Pillars is rejected by the draft board
summary: After telling the examining officers about his band's free shows for the troops, Pillars is rejected from the Army and is happy to be.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: In the meantime, the Army was gradually taking fellows. I've had several guys -- I'd call up, they would say Yes, they could join the band, and then they'd call back and say they received their greetings. '43 was a rough year, personnel-wise. But we stuck it out. And we stuck it out. In the meantime, my draft board called me in, and I had to go down to the Jefferson Barracks to be examined. I was examined and they passed me on through. When I got to the last post, I was talking to a captain and a major. And they asked me what did I think of the Army. I told them I thought the Army was a wonderful institution. I said, 'You gentlemen are doing your part, and I might as well do my part like you and everybody else.'

I told him, I said, 'To prove to you that I've tried to do my part, the night before last, I brought my band and my show down here to entertain all the troops down here, and I come down here -- been coming down here twice a month, for the last year.' And the major said, 'Was that your band?' I said, 'Yes, sir, major, that was our band.'

So they went in a huddle, and I was looking out the window. And they came back and told me, said, 'Pillars, I guess you'll still be leading the band.' I said, 'Okay,' and I went on downstairs, waiting for them to call me to go to the Army, and

I was the last one they called. And they said, 'Hayes Pillars, come upstairs, reject.' So I was rejected. I don't know why, but maybe since the gentlemen found out I was playing out there, every two weeks bringing the whole show and band out there, they figured my services were worth something for staying out of the Army. And naturally -- I'm going to be honest -- I was happy, and glad that I didn't have to go.
And I went back home, I grabbed my little wife and hugged her, and I must say, that was a very happy day for me.

Was I close to 38, then? No, I was 35 years old. 35, that was '41 -- no, 35, 41 --
Well, yes, maybe that helped, too. Maybe that helped, too. Anyway, I walked back on the bandstand that night, everybody was surprised to see me. They said, 'Oh, no, not you.' I said, 'Yes, it is me.'
But we had to sweat through with whatever musicians we had to make it.
